edits.find: When X released core components of its ranking logic through the official X recommendation algorithm repository on GitHub, it confirmed that timeline population is not a simple chronological query. Instead, it is a multi-stage machine learning pipeline that filters hundreds of millions of daily posts down to a personalized selection of several hundred updates per user.
edits.replace: X first published parts of its ranking code in 2023 in the twitter/the-algorithm repository on GitHub, and has since published a newer version of its For You feed system in the xai-org/x-algorithm repository (Apache 2.0 licence, updated as recently as October 2026). Both confirm that the For You feed is not chronological: it is a multi-stage pipeline that gathers candidate posts, filters them, and ranks them for each viewer.

edits.find: According to technical specifications published in the X Engineering publication on recommendation architecture, the recommendation pipeline executes in three primary stages:
edits.replace: According to the README of the current repository, the pipeline works roughly as follows:
edits.reason: Replaced 2023 blog (blocked/outdated) with current primary source

edits.find:
• Candidate Sourcing: The recommendation system extracts approximately 1,500 candidate posts from a pool of hundreds of millions. This candidate pool is divided roughly equally between "In-Network" posts (content from accounts the user already follows) and "Out-of-Network" posts (content from accounts the user does not follow, discovered via graph embeddings and community clustering).
  • Heavy Ranking (Transformer Neural Scoring): A core neural network evaluates each candidate post across dozens of probability features. It calculates the likelihood that a user will interact positively (replying, reposting, liking, or dwelling) versus negatively (blocking, muting, reporting, or requesting fewer posts).
  • Visibility Filtering & Heuristics: In the final stage, safety filters, content deduplication, author diversity rules, and fatigue heuristics are applied. This ensures a user's feed is not monopolized by multiple consecutive updates from a single creator or flooded with low-relevance automated replies.
edits.replace:
• Candidate Sourcing: In-network posts come from accounts the viewer follows. Out-of-network posts are retrieved by an embedding model that matches viewers with similar posts, by community clusters (SimClusters), and from a list of recent popular posts.
  • Pre-Scoring Filters: Duplicates, posts older than 48 hours, the viewer's own posts, and posts from blocked or muted accounts are removed.
  • Ranking: A transformer model predicts the probability of each action—likes, replies, reposts, clicks, dwell time, and negative actions such as blocks, mutes, and reports—and combines them into a single weighted score.
  • Author Diversity & Visibility: Each additional post from the same author is multiplied by a decaying factor, and visibility filtering decides whether a post is shown, shown with a notice, or dropped.
edits.reason: Pipeline description corrected to match the current published README

edits.find: For creators seeking audience expansion, the critical breakthrough occurs in Out-of-Network candidate generation. Out-of-network discovery is driven primarily by "SimClusters"—an algorithmic approach that groups users into dynamic interest clusters based on overlapping follow graphs and interaction histories. If your content demonstrates high engagement density within a specific community cluster (such as AI infrastructure, macroeconomic analysis, or Web3 tooling), the recommendation model categorizes your post as high-relevance candidates for other users mapped to that same community cluster.
edits.replace: For growth, out-of-network discovery matters most. One of its sources, SimClusters, groups accounts and posts into communities based on engagement patterns. Consistently engaging a specific community (for example, people interested in AI tooling or personal finance) makes it more likely your posts are retrieved for other users in that community.
edits.reason: Removed overstated "primarily driven" claim

edits.find: Not all user interactions contribute equally to distribution. The heavy ranker uses a weighted scoring formula where specific positive actions dramatically amplify post scores, while negative user feedback triggers punitive dampening factors. Designing posts that encourage high-value actions is the single most effective way to trigger algorithmic lift.
edits.replace: Not all interactions count equally. The ranking score is a weighted sum: each predicted action probability is multiplied by a weight, positive or negative, and the results are added together.
edits.reason: Removed hype; described the published formula

edits.find: A critical technical insight from the ranking formula is the immense value placed on author-engaged conversation threads. When a user comments on your post and you post a substantive response, the algorithm interprets the exchange as high-utility conversation. A post generating 20 multi-turn comments with author responses frequently achieves greater out-of-network distribution than a post accumulating 100 passive likes with zero comments.
edits.replace: Because replies and quote posts carry the largest positive weights, and negative signals carry very large negative weights, posts that start genuine conversations—without annoying people—tend to score better than posts that only collect likes. Replying to thoughtful comments keeps those conversations going.

edits.find:
Understanding the engagement half-life of an X post helps establish an optimal routine:

  • Hours 0 to 2 (Velocity Window): Initial candidate scoring evaluates immediate impressions against follower engagement rates. This stage determines whether the post breaches the In-Network ceiling into out-of-network recommendation.
  • Hours 2 to 12 (Algorithmic Expansion): Posts with strong reply depth and high dwell time are distributed into interest clusters (SimClusters) across global time zones.
  • Hours 12 to 48 (Evergreen Decay): Highly bookmarked and reposted posts continue surfacing on "For You" timelines based on personalized topic affinities.
edits.replace: Because posts older than 48 hours are filtered out of For You candidates in the published code, most of a post's For You distribution happens within its first two days. Check X's analytics for your own posts to see when your audience is most active.
edits.reason: Removed invented hour-by-hour decay model

edits.find:
• Engagement Pods: Participating in artificial engagement groups where members reciprocally like and repost each other triggers coordinated inauthentic behavior filters. The algorithm monitors graph interaction clustering and degrades reach when reciprocal engagement lacks organic topic alignment.
  • Hashtag Stacking: Using three or more hashtags clutters your message and signals spam to modern classifiers. Contemporary recommendation models rely on semantic entity extraction and natural language processing; explicit hashtags are largely unnecessary for discovery.
  • Aggressive Follow-Unfollow Loops: Rapidly following and unfollowing accounts to draw curiosity triggers automated rate limits and degrades your account trust score.
  • Sensationalized Engagement Bait: Prompts like "Agree or disagree?" or "Repost if you want $1,000" may yield short-term surface metrics, but high user mute/block rates severely degrade your long-term heavy ranker scoring.
edits.replace:
• Engagement Pods: Groups where members automatically like and repost each other may conflict with X's platform-manipulation and spam rules, and engagement from unrelated accounts teaches the system the wrong audience for your posts.
  • Hashtag Stacking: Piling on hashtags clutters your message and adds little.
  • Aggressive Follow-Unfollow Loops: Rapid following and unfollowing is a classic spam pattern and can get an account limited.
  • Sensationalized Engagement Bait: Prompts like "Repost if you want $1,000" may lift surface metrics briefly, but mutes, blocks, “not interested” clicks, and reports carry large negative weights in the published ranking parameters.
edits.reason: Removed unverifiable mechanism claims; tied engagement-bait point to verified weights
